summary.title: Fixed vs. Growth: The Two Basic Mindsets That Shape Our Lives
summary.one_liner: Carol Dweck's research shows how a fixed mindset (abilities are static) versus a growth mindset (abilities can be developed) shapes behavior, learning, relationships, and how we handle failure and effort.
keywords: mindset: the new psychology of success
takeaways: A fixed mindset treats intelligence and character as static, so success becomes proof of talent and failure becomes a verdict on it.
A growth mindset treats failure and effort as opportunities to learn and develop abilities.
Praising children for effort rather than innate ability led to more interest in challenge, better performance on harder problems, and less dishonesty in Dweck's studies.
Fixed-mindset people tend to see conflicts in relationships as fixed character flaws, while growth-mindset people see them as communication problems to work on.
summary.summary: This Brain Pickings essay by Maria Popova summarizes Stanford psychologist Carol Dweck's research, synthesized in her book Mindset: The New Psychology of Success. It contrasts fixed and growth mindsets across professional, educational, and romantic contexts, drawing on studies with four-year-olds, adolescents, and adults, including the praise-for-ability versus praise-for-effort experiments. The article is a reading summary built from quotes and study descriptions rather than a how-to guide.
